stories.headline: Severe weather diverts 22 flights from DIA to Colorado Springs, injures one passenger
stories.summary:
Nearly two dozen flights were diverted from Denver International Airport to Colorado Springs on Monday as severe weather struck the metro area, according to Colorado Springs Airport officials. Four international and 18 domestic flights were redirected, with the first arriving at 4:40 p.m. and the last touching down around 8 p.m. All diverted aircraft departed Colorado Springs by 10 p.m.

At least five passengers required medical evaluations after encountering significant turbulence during their diversions. Colorado Springs Fire Department paramedics transported one person to a hospital with unspecified injuries. Airport spokesperson Aidan Ryan noted that Colorado Springs serves as the primary diversion airport for DIA, particularly during summer months when unstable weather conditions are common.

Beyond the diversions, Monday's storms caused widespread disruption at DIA, delaying 853 flights and canceling 44, according to FlightAware tracking data. Delays were split nearly evenly between arriving and departing flights, though the majority of cancellations affected outbound departures.

stories.headline: Wildfire smoke triggers air quality advisory for all Colorado counties; temperatures expected to rebound to triple digits by weekend
stories.summary:
Out-of-state wildfires sent waves of smoke across Colorado on Tuesday, prompting the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment to issue an air quality health advisory covering every county in the state through at least 9 a.m. Wednesday. Smoke was arriving from multiple directions — fires in Utah and Nevada pushing in from the west, and fires in other upwind states drifting into northeast Colorado.

A cold front that moved through Monday night drove temperatures in Denver from a record-breaking 102-degree high down to an overnight low of 57 degrees, but the same weather system drew cold, dense air that carried wildfire smoke closer to the surface. National Weather Service meteorologist Abby Pettett said smoke from Pacific Northwest fires compounded the air quality problems already caused by western fires.

Near-surface smoke is expected to begin lifting Wednesday as conditions gradually improve, while upper-level smoke causing hazy skies may start to diminish by Thursday. Temperatures are forecast to climb back into the 90s by Thursday and potentially reach triple digits again over the weekend, which would approach or break several August daily records in Denver.

stories.headline: Denver records second-hottest July in city history, with 28 days at 90 degrees or above
stories.summary:
Denver's July 2026 ranked as the second-warmest July ever recorded in the city, with a monthly average temperature of 78.7 degrees, according to the National Weather Service. The record belongs to July 2012, which logged a 78.9-degree average. The city saw 28 days with temperatures reaching 90 degrees or higher, itself a record for the most such days in a single July.

Denver hit triple digits three times during the month, with the hottest day occurring July 26 at a record-breaking 103 degrees. Two additional 100-degree days have already been logged in August, placing 2026 in a five-way tie for fourth place among years with the most triple-digit days on record. Three more such days would move the city into second place on that list, behind only 2012's 13 days of triple-digit heat.

The historically hot summer comes amid a deepening statewide drought and follows months of elevated temperatures across the region. Forecasters expect temperatures to return to the 90s later this week and potentially challenge additional daily records over the weekend.

stories.headline: Federal judge dismisses Trump administration lawsuit against Colorado over voter roll data, with prejudice
stories.summary:
A Denver-based U.S. District Court judge on Tuesday dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against Colorado seeking access to sensitive voter data, ruling that the Department of Justice failed to provide sufficient justification for obtaining unredacted voter information and is not entitled to it under federal law. Judge Philip Brimmer, a George W. Bush appointee, dismissed the case with prejudice, meaning the DOJ cannot refile it.

The lawsuit stemmed from a DOJ request last year demanding that Colorado and other states turn over election records including driver's license numbers and the last four digits of voters' Social Security numbers. Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold declined to comply, citing both legal concerns and a 2024 state law that blocks release of sensitive personal data. The state did provide the DOJ with publicly available copies of the master voter file.

Griswold and other Democratic election officials said they were concerned the Trump administration intended to use the sensitive data to check voters' citizenship status. The administration had defended the request by arguing that accurate voter rolls are essential to fair elections and that states had fallen into a pattern of noncompliance with voter roll maintenance requirements. A request for comment from the White House was not immediately returned.

stories.headline: DCCC adds Colorado's 3rd and 4th congressional districts to its competitive races target list
stories.summary:
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has added Colorado's 3rd and 4th congressional districts to its list of districts considered competitive for the upcoming election cycle, according to the Colorado Sun. The move signals that national Democrats see pickup opportunities in two districts that have historically leaned Republican.

Colorado's 3rd Congressional District, which covers the vast western and southern portions of the state, and the 4th District, covering the eastern plains and southern Front Range, have both been represented by Republicans in recent years. The DCCC designation typically brings increased national attention, fundraising support, and campaign infrastructure to targeted races.

The addition comes amid a broader competitive environment on Colorado's congressional map, where Democratic challengers have been actively fundraising and recruiting in districts once considered safely Republican.

stories.headline: Broncos release updated Burnham Yard district renderings as stadium planning continues
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos on Tuesday released updated renderings of their proposed multi-use district surrounding a potential new stadium at the Burnham Yard site, offering the public the latest vision for more than 100 acres of land near the defunct rail yard in Denver. The renderings, designed by Denver-based architecture firm Tryba, do not include images of the stadium itself — team president Damani Leech said those are still some time away as approvals and negotiations continue.

Key changes in the updated district plan include eliminating a vehicle crossing at 11th Avenue to improve pedestrian and bike safety, expanding public green space to approximately 11 to 12 acres, removing freight rail tracks in favor of a tree-lined trail, and closing additional crossings on event days. The team says the revisions incorporate extensive input from community groups gathered over nearly a year since Burnham Yard was announced as the preferred site.

Leech noted that global architecture firm Manica has been working on stadium designs for several months, with Broncos ownership described as closely involved in that process. The Burnham Yard master plan has been through multiple iterations since Sasaki completed initial planning work earlier this year, and the team acknowledged the process continues to evolve amid ongoing community and city negotiations.

stories.headline: Rockies trade reliever Victor Vodnik to Marlins for infielder Connor Norby and pitching prospect Aiden May
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies made a trade deadline move Tuesday, acquiring infielder Connor Norby and Minor League right-handed pitcher Aiden May from the Miami Marlins in exchange for reliever Victor Vodnik. The deal adds infield depth to a Rockies roster that has struggled throughout the 2026 season.

Norby, 26, is a versatile infielder who has appeared in 198 Major League games with Miami, posting a career slash line of .234/.302/.383 with 21 home runs and 70 RBI. He has played third base, first base, second base, and designated hitter during his career, giving Colorado flexibility across the lineup. May, 23, is a Minor League starter who posted a 3.80 ERA across 14 starts at High-A Beloit this season.

Vodnik, 26, leaves Colorado after parts of four seasons with the club, compiling a 13-10 record, 4.31 ERA, and 23 saves in a Rockies uniform. He was 3-3 with a 5.25 ERA in 33 appearances this season before the trade. The Rockies now carry 38 players on their 40-man roster.

stories.headline: Nikola Jokic's unsigned extension has league-wide attention on Denver Nuggets' future
stories.summary:
NBA insider Marc Stein revealed on the DNVR Nuggets Podcast that the Denver Nuggets have become one of the most closely watched franchises across the league this offseason, driven largely by uncertainty surrounding Nikola Jokic's contract extension status. Jokic, the franchise cornerstone and three-time MVP, has now declined to sign an extension for the second consecutive summer.

"There are a lot of eyeballs on the Denver Nuggets right now league-wide," Stein said. "There is a lot of curiosity about where this team is going and, let's face it, Jokic could have signed an extension for the second straight summer and did not." Stein noted that even if the decision is entirely driven by financial considerations, it will continue to fuel speculation and monitoring by rival franchises.

The situation adds to an already uncertain offseason for Denver, which has also been navigating sign-and-trade discussions involving Peyton Watson with the Atlanta Hawks. The Nuggets remain a title contender on paper, but Jokic's contract situation has elevated the franchise to a central storyline entering the 2026-27 season.

stories.headline: Boulder County sheriff seeks driver caught on camera speeding down Highway 36 bike path
stories.summary:
The Boulder County Sheriff's Office is searching for a driver after video captured a car speeding down the bike path adjacent to U.S. Highway 36 in Boulder County over the weekend. The incident was recorded on camera and shared by authorities as they seek to identify and locate the responsible driver.

Details on the vehicle's speed, the specific location along Highway 36, and whether any cyclists or pedestrians were endangered were not immediately available in the initial report. The sheriff's office has not announced any arrests in connection with the incident.

The Highway 36 corridor between Denver and Boulder is a heavily used route for cyclists and pedestrians, and a vehicle operating on the path poses a significant public safety hazard. Authorities urged anyone with information about the driver's identity to contact the Boulder County Sheriff's Office.

stories.headline: Denver rolls out new rules targeting neglected properties, with significantly steeper penalties for owners
stories.summary:
Denver is implementing new regulations this month aimed at addressing neglected and blighted properties more quickly, with substantially increased financial penalties for property owners who fail to take corrective action, according to Denver7. The rules are designed to accelerate enforcement timelines compared to the city's previous process.

Specific penalty amounts and the categories of property violations covered under the new rules were not fully detailed in the initial report, but the changes signal a more aggressive posture from the city on property maintenance compliance. Denver has faced longstanding criticism from neighborhoods and community groups over slow enforcement of blight and neglect complaints.

The new rules take effect this month, and city officials indicated the changes represent a meaningful shift in how Denver approaches properties that generate ongoing complaints or pose neighborhood concerns.

stories.headline: Former Colorado governor donates career papers to Metropolitan State University of Denver
stories.summary:
A former Colorado governor has donated his career papers to Metropolitan State University of Denver, according to CPR News, which reported the governor also reflected on his life growing up in a small Colorado town during the Dust Bowl era. The donation preserves a significant collection of historical records related to Colorado's political history at a Denver-based public institution.

Metropolitan State University of Denver, located in downtown Denver, houses various archival collections tied to Colorado history and public affairs. The addition of a former governor's career papers represents a notable acquisition for the university's historical holdings.

Further details on which former governor made the donation and the scope of the collection were not immediately available from the initial report.

stories.headline: Denver weather brings sharp temperature swing: 102-degree record Monday followed by smoky 73-degree Tuesday
stories.summary:
Denver experienced a dramatic temperature swing this week as a cold front dropped the city from a record-breaking high of 102 degrees on Monday to a high of just 73 degrees on Tuesday — the coolest day since June 25, according to the National Weather Service and Denver Gazette. The abrupt cool-down came alongside gusty winds and widespread wildfire smoke visible across the metro area.

The same winds driving the cooler temperatures carried smoke from ongoing Utah wildfires Monday, transitioning to smoke from Pacific Northwest fires by Tuesday. Residents were advised to limit strenuous outdoor activity, with health officials recommending walks instead of runs and other modifications to exercise routines during the air quality advisory.

The cool stretch is expected to be brief, with temperatures forecast to climb back into the 80s Wednesday and return to the 90s by Thursday. Forecasters warned that triple-digit heat could return as early as the weekend, potentially challenging additional daily temperature records in Denver.

topStory.headline: Spokane Man Charged With Arson as Washington Wildfires Destroy Hundreds of Structures, Force 67,000 to Evacuate
topStory.summary:
Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, Washington, was arrested Monday and charged with first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire, the largest of three major wildfires burning through the Spokane region. Together, the three blazes have destroyed at least 700 structures, burned more than 8,000 acres and forced approximately 67,000 people to evacuate. As of Tuesday morning, none of the fires had been contained.

Farinacci was taken into custody without incident with the assistance of a SWAT team after a judge signed an arrest warrant. Authorities said a witness reported seeing a man matching Farinacci's description near the origin point of the Old Trails Fire shortly before it ignited around 10 a.m. Saturday, crouching in grass at the side of a road before standing up and walking away nervously. Deputies detained Farinacci the same day approximately a half-mile from where the fire started and found him in possession of waterproof matches and a butane lighter, but released him. By Sunday, major crimes detectives had linked him to the fire and determined that the fire's point of origin corresponded exactly to where witnesses had seen him kneeling. His bond was set at $1 million, and he was scheduled to make his first court appearance Tuesday.

Farinacci has a significant criminal history. He pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault in Maricopa County, Arizona, for the 2010 shooting death of his father at their Mesa home. He served approximately a decade in prison. Spokane County Prosecuting Attorney Preston McCollam said Farinacci had also been questioned in connection with arson-related behavior in the past, though he was never arrested or charged. Court documents show he was contacted by law enforcement during two separate fire investigations in 2025 — once in July near his apartment along the Spokane River and once in August during a wildfire investigation at Riverside State Park, where he was found on a park bench appearing out of breath and wearing a green T-shirt similar to the one he wore on Saturday.

Sheriff John Nowels said there is no evidence connecting Farinacci to the other two fires burning in the region. Investigators said Tuesday that the other two blazes were also human-caused, though not necessarily intentional, with exact causes still under investigation. No deaths have been reported. Cooler and calmer weather aided firefighting efforts Tuesday, though hotter, drier and windier conditions are forecast later in the week, raising concern that the fires could grow before they are brought under control.
